The solution for May 28, 2026 (Day 1525) is Ebony. The hex code is #313337. This falls squarely into the dark-neutral hue family. After three days of saturated colors like Velvet and Cadet, the puzzle demands a shift to near-black tones.

Ebony is a deep, flat neutral. It lacks the blue undertones of Storm or the purple tint of Velvet. The hex values for red, green, and blue are 49, 51, and 55 respectively. These numbers are so close they effectively cancel out any color bias.

This makes Ebony one of the trickiest neutrals to land on. It sits just above pure black (#000000) but far below mid-gray. If your guess is too light, you get a yellow hint for value. Too dark, and you get nothing. The margin for error is razor-thin.

Since the recent history includes Cadet and Storm, many players will instinctively guess blue-heavy colors. Ignore that pattern. The puzzle has reset to neutral. Use a color with zero saturation to confirm the hue family before adjusting the lightness.

The most common mistake is guessing a blue-black or brown-black. The human eye often perceives dark neutrals as having a tint, but Ebony is strictly neutral. Guessing #000033 or #330000 will waste a turn because the hue is completely wrong.

Another pitfall is overshooting the value. Players see "dark" and jump straight to #000000. Ebony is slightly lighter than that. You need to find the specific band between 30 and 40 on the RGB scale. Guessing pure black leaves you with no data on the exact shade.

The color feedback system treats neutral colors differently than saturated ones. When you guess a color with low saturation, the game prioritizes value hints over hue hints. This means your first few guesses should focus on getting the brightness right.

Once the value is locked in (indicated by a green value hint), the hue feedback becomes the only variable. Since Ebony has almost no hue, the game will signal this by returning gray or neutral hints for color, confirming you are looking for a flat tone.

Because Ebony is a neutral. It contains no blue, red, or green dominance. A blue guess like Storm (#000B44) will show zero green hints for hue, only value feedback if the darkness matches.

How to read the visual hints

Each RGB value runs from 0 to 255. A color at (255, 0, 0) is pure red; (0, 0, 0) is black; (255, 255, 255) is white. When you see the target color, mentally break it apart: which channels carry the most intensity? Which are muted or absent?

The hint system doesn't tell you exact numbers—it shows you relative warmth, coolness, and luminance. If the target skews yellow, expect high red and green values with minimal blue. A purple target means strong blue with significant red but little green.

For darker targets, remember you're working with additive mixing. You can't subtract—you can only add more of one channel to push toward the goal. Check the archive link above for past puzzles if you want to see how different difficulty levels present their hints.

Common wrong approaches

Players coming from paint mixing often assume cyan + magenta = purple. In additive RGB mixing, that's backwards. Cyan comes from green + blue, and magenta comes from red + blue. Getting this foundation wrong will derail every guess.

Another frequent mistake: treating gray targets as needing "equal" RGB values. Gray at mid-intensity isn't necessarily (128, 128, 128)—it depends on whether the target skews warm or cool. Look for subtle bias even in neutral colors.

Some players overthink saturation while ignoring brightness. A highly saturated bright color needs high values across multiple channels, not just vivid hues. The solver tool linked above can help verify your reasoning once you've landed on a combination.

Questions players keep asking

Does the order of my three colors matter?

No. The game adds all three RGB values together regardless of sequence. What matters is the final sum matching the target.

Can I reuse a color in the same guess?

Yes. Using the same value twice—like (200, 100, 100)—is legal and sometimes necessary for certain targets.

What's the difference between hard mode and normal mode?

In hard mode, any color you guess must appear somewhere in your previous attempts. Normal mode lets you guess freely. Check your settings if you're unsure which mode you're playing.

Why did my correct-looking guess get marked wrong?

RGB mixing rounds values internally. A guess that looks right visually might be off by a few points per channel. The game uses precise math—not just eyeballing—to evaluate your answer.

Difficulty varies based on target color complexity. Highly saturated primaries tend to be easier; desaturated neutrals with subtle biases catch more players off guard. Use the daily archive to compare patterns across recent puzzles.

Dotadle answer today: which hero clues carry the most weight

The primary attribute clue is your sharpest filter. If today's board shows an attribute hint, treat it as non-negotiable. Strength heroes tend toward high HP pools and tanky builds, Agility heroes scale with attack speed and armor, Intelligence heroes rely on mana and abilities, and Universal heroes blend these profiles. Knowing which category you're hunting changes how aggressively you can prune the remaining candidates. The attribute clue appears early in most Dotadle sessions precisely because it's so decisive—don't sleep on it by saving it for last.

How to cut the Dota roster faster

The full Dota 2 hero pool exceeds 120 characters. That's too many to brute-force. Instead, build a mental elimination sequence: start with attribute, then apply role constraints, then check lane viability. Role clues—Carry, Support, Offlane, Soft Support—narrow further but watch for overlap. Many heroes flex across roles depending on draft context. Anti-Mage functions as hard carry but can slip into aggressive offlane against the right matchup. Shadow Fiend tops the damage charts as a position-one hero but sees occasional use as a farming mid. This flexibility trips up players who treat role labels as rigid buckets.

Lane assignment helps most when combined with attribute data. A Strength hero marked for safe lane likely means a tanky frontliner or sustain-focused carry. An Agility hero assigned to the offlane probably signals a slippery initiator or split-pusher. Intelligence heroes in the support role usually point toward disable-heavy playmakers. A glowing blue hero could be Riki (Agility) or Crystal Maiden (Intelligence). A massive armored figure might be Tidehunter (Strength) or Dragon Knight (also Strength, but the attribute distinction still matters more than the silhouette similarity).

Lane assignment proves most reliable for core positions and least reliable for supports. Position-five heroes cover the widest hero pool and show up in every lane rotation depending on the game's flow. Hard supports like Lion, Lich, and CM have predictable patterns, but roamers and position-four supports blur those lines constantly. When lane clues feel ambiguous, lean back on attribute filtering and let the roster collapse naturally.

Tomorrow's puzzle will reset the clue stack, but your process shouldn't. Build a consistent reading order: attribute first, then role, then lane, then secondary traits. This habit pays dividends across multiple rounds and keeps you from chasing dead ends down visual rabbit holes.

Globle answer today: what the heat clues point to first

The heat widget on today's board gives you two things: a color and a direction to explore. Most players fixate on finding the hottest shade and miss the directional pattern underneath. Watch what happens when you push north versus south, east versus west. If moving north consistently drops the temperature, the mystery country sits south of your current position. Start with a central country on each continent you're willing to test. For Africa, that might mean Nigeria or Kenya. For South America, Colombia or Brazil works. How to read warm guesses without rushing

A warm result—yellow or light orange—tells you the mystery country sits in your general region. It does not tell you which neighboring country to try next. Instead, use warm guesses to establish a perimeter. Test countries that are perpendicular to your current position. If you're warm on Argentina, try Chile or Brazil before cycling through every Argentine neighbor. You're mapping a zone, not following a checklist.

Where the map logic usually breaks down

The most common mistake players make is treating the heat map like a GPS distance meter. Geographic distance on a sphere doesn't map cleanly to visual proximity on a flat screen. Countries that look far apart on your monitor might share maritime borders or sit very close across a strait. Countries that look adjacent might be separated by thousands of miles of ocean.

Another failure point: anchoring on the first warm guess. Once something registers as hot, players tunnel toward it and stop exploring broadly. But the mystery country could sit on the opposite side of that warm zone. You need at least three data points before committing to a search quadrant.

Map projections distort polar regions particularly badly.
